I have several 20x Max subscriptions. I have no way to measure total token usage because most of my sessions are cloud session but they’ve been using the same automated workflow across similar projects.

One account, which was subscribed most recently, uses up about 15% of its weekly quota in a single maxed out five hour session. The other accounts use up nearly 30% for a full five hour session, meaning I get several less days less of use overall from those subs.

Is Anthropic pulling more shenanigans with their subscriptions again?

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 23:29:03 +0000https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50252654throwup238https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50252654https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50252654<![CDATA[Ask HN: Why Is Anthropic's Customer Support Bad?]]>I've been a Max user of Claude all year and it's crucial to my day to day work. Last night I had a new experience which makes me feel like a junior dev who blew thousands of dollars on a misconfigured AWS CDK file.

To avoid agents doing online research from leaking private info I created a persona which can do online research as a subagent from a fresh context, I asked it to fact check claims as well. Little did I know subagents don't report their token usage and my subagents ended up recursively checking claims. I burned through 80% of my Fable usage for the week in 10 minutes.

I've never come close to using my full token allowance before and now I'm going to have to spend money on expensive usage tokens or upgrade to 20x (or change to a different provider) to complete this weeks work.

Anthropic's online support agent was terse, "empathizing" but ultimately said it could not do anything.

Wouldn't the right thing from a Customer Support perspective to give a one-time usage reset in a case like this? If they had a human instead of an agent doing it, would that have changed the outcome?

I've implemented bounding now in my persona's but it just seems like this is a preventable problem that they're (1) not solving and (2) not willing to remedy when it did happen.

Full disclosure, I love what Anthropic has built in Claude and use the product daily.

Running several agents at the same time, I found myself having a hard time catching up on everything produced, and giving proper feedback. I tend to actually ask my agent to go through transcripts to find old unfinished tasks and re-state the outputs.

MD files became tedious, screen shots didn't show the entire flow, production code was usually stale or on stuck on a branch.

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:32:39 +0000https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245483reacharavindhhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245483https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245483<![CDATA[Why it is foolish to think AI can't write like humans]]>Last I counted there were 50+ AI text detectors, not including the humanizers that also sell AI detection (thank you hypocrisy). What's even more surprising is the AI built meters and percentage scores they provide when you enter a text. A load of bollocks if you ask me. Working on AI linguistics if there is something you learn, anything is possible with the right technique and framework. I'm not sure what is more concerning the display of such banality or the actual belief in them, nonetheless, the challenge must be addressed.

There are mostly 2 types of value systems on this, the first is that AI is supreme and will be able to replace human output (or already has) and the second, that AI can never be human. Both are true, to an extent. AI could never be human because what it means to be human is so loosely defined, that there will always be an argument to prove the point for the point's sake. In this context, AI can surely write like humans - and it is mostly humans guiding it in getting there. The point is not whether the writing is human or AI, which can never be certain. It's the grey area of doubt that you can find clues on, for further investigation or reason.

The point of this note is to warn you against looking at symbolic meters and percentage scores. Here's a quick test you can do to evaluate a score (we do this too), copy 200 words from an AI model and test it. Note the percentage, then replace 2 meaningful words at random and note the percentage difference. If 2 words causes a big shift, it's highly sensitive - you can infer that it would not hold up against real world testing. If it doesn't shift much, randomly shuffle the sentences and retry - if it shifts, you have your answer. The reasoning is that if it is truly accurate measure of writing as is, it would give consistent % scores on the same text, no matter how it's sliced. If it's purely for show, it will give wildly different outcomes. Do not base your outcome on running the same text multiple times without changing it, as most detectors will probably use a cached result rather than re-evaluate - lest it makes them look unreliable. As anyone who works with data will tell you, there will always be outliers.

In short, treat detector results as flags and do get carried away by a false sense of UI assurance. Interfaces and widgets look flashy, look underneath. AI can most certainly write like humans (especially when guided by them), it would be foolish to think otherwise.

Taken from https://t9xt.com/writings/why-it-is-foolish-to-think-ai-can-t-write-like-humans

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:05:12 +0000https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245017nitishrhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245017https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50245017<![CDATA[Ask HN: How bad is AI hurting recruitment, from both sides?]]>Hi Folks, Having been on the applicant side of hiring late, I've notice a lot of similar posts from people in the same situation (frequency illusion ?), due to the volume of applications they are unsure their CV is reviewed by human eyes.

Separately, I've started reaching out to hiring managers, recruiters, agencies etc to get their input. There has been a common thread in their response, AI is used to review and "grade" submissions but its not uncommon for lower graded submissions to actually get the job over higher graded submissions.

A few are using off the shelf software, others have created their own harness. We are seemingly in the world of applicants using AI to help apply, and AI grading the submissions. With Pandora's box opened, it's difficult to see AI ever being completely removed from the process, but it feels like a vicious cycle.

(Job Market is tough -> People using AI to apply (sometimes auto apply) to jobs with targeted, enhanced or fabricated CVs -> Job openings receiving increased and overwhelming number of applications -> using AI to help filter and reduce the noise -> repeat).

For people hiring, are you seeing the same? Do CV's carry the same weight as they use to and are screen calls now a necessary requirement? For people applying, how often are getting feedback & are far are you tailoring your CV?

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:43:07 +0000https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50243565abalgirhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50243565https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50243565<![CDATA[AI is coming for accounting after coding]]>Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. writing contracts is where an LLM shines, it's basic building blocks are formal words. Formal is the key term here.

Accounting if different. More precise, it tolerates less mistakes. The rules that govern it are much less open to intrepretation.

In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future.

In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate.

It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. Accounting follows the same power law as football. In a 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad journal entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal:

1. In those two, a task would not be ruined by a single mistake in the system. An app would run fine with a couple of bugs if the system design was decent. A contract would still be enforceable with an additional weak sentence in most cases. But in accounting, 1 digit error would ruin the entire balance sheet.

2. The cost of making a mistake. Worst case scenario, the system goes down for a couple of hours, you might lose a case because of a bad contract. But losing track of the financials is a different story, it can easily destroy the whole company.

3. Trust is harder to establish with accounting. You can outsource legal without understanding much about the law. But if you outsource accounting without understanding the numbers; you are toast.

Also, all the major labs are going after it soon, margins are going down fast.

Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story.

Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller.
